units.t: First Aid & Safety. Episode one.
In this episode: CPR: how to save a life, Choking: back blows and chest thrusts, Stopping severe bleeding and Heart attack and stroke: spotting the signs.
Part one. CPR: how to save a life.
When someone's heart stops, the next few minutes decide everything.
Anyone can help, and doing something is always better than doing nothing.
Arrest and the action plan.
A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle; the person is usually awake and in pain.
Cardiac arrest is different: the heart's rhythm fails and it stops pumping, and the person collapses and stops breathing normally.
Brain damage starts within minutes, and survival falls with every minute without CPR.
In Australia only around one in ten people survive an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but prompt CPR and defibrillation by bystanders improve those odds greatly.
The ANZCOR action plan is DRSABCD.
Check Danger.
Check Response.
Send for help: call Triple Zero, 000, use speaker, and send someone for a defibrillator.
Open the Airway.
Check Breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Start CPR.
Attach a Defibrillator when it arrives.
Gasping is not breathing.
One big reason bystanders hesitate is uncertainty about breathing.
In the first minutes of cardiac arrest, many people make slow, irregular gasping or snoring sounds, called agonal breathing.
It can look like breathing, but it isn't effective, and it is a sign of cardiac arrest.
ANZCOR guidance is clear: if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR.
Don't waste time searching for a pulse; it is unreliable even for trained people.
If you start CPR on someone who turns out not to need it, the risk of harm is low.
The risk of waiting is far higher.
Compressions and breaths.
Kneel beside the person, on their back on a firm surface.
Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone, other hand on top, arms straight.
Press down about one third of the chest depth and let it fully rise.
Aim for 100 to 120 compressions a minute; the beat of 'Stayin' Alive' is about right.
Ribs may crack.
Keep going: a broken rib heals, but a stopped heart doesn't restart on its own.
The standard ratio is 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths.
Tilt the head back, lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs and blow for about a second, watching the chest rise.
If you are untrained, unable or unwilling to give breaths, ANZCOR advises continuous compressions alone.
Defibrillators and children.
An automated external defibrillator, or AED, analyses the heart's rhythm and delivers a shock only if it detects a rhythm that can be corrected.
You don't need training: switch it on and follow the spoken instructions.
Expose the chest, dry it if wet, stick the pads where pictured and stand clear when told.
Resume CPR immediately afterwards.
AEDs are found in shopping centres, gyms, sporting clubs and workplaces, and using one within minutes can dramatically increase survival.
For a child, use the heel of one or two hands; for an infant under one, two fingers.
Press about one third of the chest depth.
Use paediatric pads if available, otherwise adult pads.
If others are there, swap every two minutes or so, and continue until the person responds, paramedics take over or you can't go on.
Don't let fear stop you.
Many people worry they will do it wrong or be sued.
Someone in cardiac arrest has no effective circulation, so your CPR can only improve their chances.
Good Samaritan laws in the Australian states and territories generally protect people who help in good faith.
If you are unsure, call Triple Zero, 000: the operator will talk you through each step.
Once the person starts breathing normally, place them in the recovery position and watch them closely.
This lesson is general information, not a substitute for training.
A first aid course, ideally refreshed every year for CPR, gives you hands-on practice and the confidence to act.
The key idea: In cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping, survival falls with every minute without CPR, and the Australian action plan is DRSABCD.
Part two. Choking: back blows and chest thrusts.
Most people picture the Heimlich manoeuvre.
Australian first aid guidelines teach something different, and the reason is a surprising story about evidence.
A silent emergency.
Movies make choking loud, but a person with a fully blocked airway usually can't speak, cough or breathe.
They may clutch their throat, look panicked, and their lips and face may turn blue or grey.
The brain is starved of oxygen within minutes, so the response must be fast.
Choking is a risk at every age.
Toddlers explore with their mouths, and grapes, nuts, popcorn and hard lollies are common culprits.
Older adults are at risk too, especially when swallowing has weakened after a stroke or with conditions such as dementia.
Meat is a classic cause in adults.
Coughing is good news.
The simplest test is whether the person can cough effectively.
A strong, noisy cough means air is still moving, and coughing is the body's best tool for clearing the airway.
Encourage them to keep coughing.
Don't slap their back or give them water while they cough well.
Stay with them and watch closely, because a partial blockage can become a complete one.
If coughing doesn't clear it, call Triple Zero, 000.
A weak, silent or ineffective cough, difficulty breathing or an inability to speak signals a severe blockage.
Then you act and call for help at the same time.
Back blows first.
Under Australian guidelines from the Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation, ANZCOR, the first step for a conscious adult or child with severe choking is back blows.
Call 000, or have someone else call.
Stand slightly behind the person, support their chest with one hand and bend them well forward, so gravity helps.
With the heel of your other hand, give a sharp blow between the shoulder blades.
Check after each blow whether the object has come out, rather than automatically delivering all five.
The aim is a sudden jolt that loosens the blockage so it falls forward out of the mouth, not deeper.
Then chest thrusts.
If five back blows haven't cleared the airway, switch to chest thrusts.
Support the person's back with one hand.
Place the heel of your other hand on the lower half of the breastbone, the same spot used for CPR, and push in sharply.
Chest thrusts are slower and sharper than CPR compressions.
Each one squeezes a burst of air out of the lungs, like a cough you create for them.
Check after each thrust.
If the blockage remains after five, go back to five back blows, and keep alternating until the object comes out, help arrives, or the person becomes unresponsive.
Heimlich and babies.
In 1974 the American surgeon Henry Heimlich popularised abdominal thrusts.
They are still taught in places such as the United Kingdom and United States, though advice varies.
ANZCOR's guideline says abdominal thrusts are not recommended, citing reports of life-threatening complications such as injured organs, and finds back blows and chest thrusts work with low risk.
If you live in Australia, learn the local method.
For babies under one, call 000 and lay the baby face down and head-down along your thigh or forearm, supporting the head and jaw.
Give up to five back blows, then turn them over for up to five two-finger chest thrusts, and keep alternating.
If anyone collapses and stops breathing normally, start CPR.
The key idea: Severe choking is usually silent, because a fully blocked airway leaves no air to speak, cough or breathe.
Part three. Stopping severe bleeding.
A person can lose a dangerous amount of blood in minutes.
The most powerful tool for stopping it is something everyone already owns: their hands.
Minutes matter.
An adult holds roughly five litres of blood.
A wound to a major vessel in the arm, leg, neck or groin can bleed heavily enough to become life-threatening within minutes.
Paramedics are fast, but not always fast enough, so the person beside the injured one matters most.
Bleeding is life-threatening if blood is spurting or pulsing, flowing steadily, pooling on the ground, or soaking through clothing and bandages.
First check for danger to yourself.
Then call Triple Zero, 000, or ask someone else to call while you act.
Put the phone on speaker so the operator can coach you.
Press hard.
Australian first aid guidelines are clear: direct pressure is usually the quickest and most effective way to stop bleeding.
Put a pad, such as folded cloth, gauze or a clean T-shirt, on the wound and press down hard with both hands.
If nothing is available, use bare hands.
Infection can be treated in hospital, but blood loss cannot be undone.
Lean in and use your body weight.
Keep the pressure steady rather than lifting to check, because each peek can let a fragile clot break.
Wear gloves if you have them, but don't waste time hunting for them.
Add, don't remove.
The instinct is to peel away a blood-soaked dressing and replace it.
Resist it.
Removing the first pad can tear away the clot forming underneath and restart the bleeding.
Place a second pad over the first and bind it firmly with a bandage, or keep pressing.
Help the person lie down, especially if the bleeding is from a leg or is severe, and keep the injured part still.
Lying down reduces the risk of fainting and helps blood reach the brain.
If an object such as a knife or glass is stuck in the wound, leave it.
It may be plugging the hole.
Pad around it and press on the pads either side, then call 000.
Using a tourniquet.
A tourniquet is a tight band around an arm or leg, above a wound, that cuts off blood flow to the limb.
Old first aid courses taught people to fear them.
Military experience, including in Iraq and Afghanistan, showed they save lives in catastrophic limb bleeding.
Australian guidelines now say to use one for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot control, if one is available and you are trained.
Place it a short distance above the wound, not over a joint or the wound itself, following the product's instructions, and tighten until the bleeding stops.
Note the time it was applied and tell paramedics.
Never loosen it yourself.
Shock and minor bleeds.
Even after bleeding is controlled, the body may struggle.
Shock is a dangerous drop in blood flow to the organs.
Signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, a rapid weak pulse, fast breathing, anxiety, confusion and drowsiness.
Keep the person lying down, reassure them and cover them to stop heat loss.
Give no food or drink, since they may need surgery.
If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR.
Most bleeding is minor.
Rinse small cuts, press with a clean cloth and cover.
For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for at least ten minutes.
Tilting the head back is wrong, as blood runs down the throat.
The key idea: Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes, so act while you call 000.
Part four. Heart attack and stroke: spotting the signs.
Heart attacks and strokes are medical emergencies where every minute counts.
Recognising the warning signs, and calling for help fast, can save a life or prevent lifelong disability.
Time is muscle.
A man feels heavy pressure in his chest while mowing the lawn and tells himself it is indigestion.
A woman notices her husband's speech is slurred at dinner, but he says he is just tired.
Scenes like these happen in Australian homes every day, and the delay can be devastating.
In a heart attack, part of the heart muscle is starved of blood.
In most strokes, part of the brain is.
The longer the blockage lasts, the more tissue dies, so doctors say 'time is muscle' for the heart and 'time is brain' for strokes.
Modern hospital treatments can open blocked vessels, but many work best when given early, which only happens if someone calls for help quickly.
Heart attack or arrest.
Your heart muscle is fed by its own blood vessels, the coronary arteries.
Over years, fatty plaque can build up inside them.
If a plaque cracks, a clot can form on top and block the artery.
The heart muscle beyond the blockage is starved of oxygen and begins to die.
Doctors call this a myocardial infarction, or heart attack.
It is different from a cardiac arrest, though the two are often confused.
In a cardiac arrest, the heart's electrical rhythm goes haywire and it stops pumping effectively, so the person collapses, stops breathing normally and becomes unresponsive.
A heart attack can trigger a cardiac arrest, which is one reason it must never be ignored or treated as something to wait out.
Heart attack: signs and action.
The Heart Foundation describes warning signs such as pain, pressure, heaviness or tightness in the chest, which may spread to the arm, shoulder, neck, jaw or back.
Others include shortness of breath, nausea, a cold sweat and feeling light-headed.
Women, older people and people with diabetes may have less typical symptoms, such as unusual tiredness or breathlessness.
Symptoms can come and go.
If you have warning signs, stop and rest.
If they are severe, get worse quickly or last longer than 10 minutes, call Triple Zero, 000, for an ambulance.
Do not drive yourself, because paramedics can start treatment straight away.
Follow the operator's advice, including any about aspirin.
If the person collapses and is not breathing normally, start CPR and send for a defibrillator.
Untrained bystanders can use one by following its spoken instructions.
Stroke and F.A.S.T.
Most strokes are ischaemic, caused by a clot or plaque blocking an artery to the brain.
Others are haemorrhagic, where a blood vessel bursts and bleeds.
Either way, brain cells lose oxygen and die.
Researchers estimate that in a typical large stroke the brain can lose close to two million nerve cells every minute without treatment.
Hospitals can now dissolve or remove many clots, but only if the person arrives quickly.
The Stroke Foundation's F.
A.
S.
T.
test is a simple check.
Face: has the mouth drooped?
Arms: can they lift both?
Speech: is it slurred?
Time: if you see any sign, call Triple Zero, 000, straight away.
Other signs include sudden one-sided weakness, vision loss, dizziness or a severe headache.
Note when symptoms began.
Give no food or drink, and stay with them.
Mini strokes and prevention.
Sometimes stroke symptoms appear and then disappear within minutes or hours.
This is often a transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, sometimes called a mini stroke.
It can be a warning that a major stroke may follow, so it needs urgent medical attention even if the person feels fine.
For both heart attack and stroke, many risk factors can be reduced: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, physical inactivity, excess weight and heavy drinking.
Regular health checks with a GP help find problems early.
This lesson is general information, not medical advice.
For more, see the Heart Foundation, the Stroke Foundation and healthdirect.
In an emergency, always call Triple Zero, 000, and consider a first aid course, which teaches CPR and defibrillator use hands on.
The key idea: In heart attacks and strokes, delay causes damage, so calling for help quickly matters more than anything.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How does cardiac arrest differ from a heart attack?
Answer. Arrest stops the heart pumping; an attack blocks blood supply.
Question two. Why is severe choking often silent?
Answer. No air can pass, so they can't speak or cough.
Question three. Why does the person next to an injured person matter most in severe bleeding?
Answer. Help may not arrive before the blood loss is critical.
Question four. Why do doctors say 'time is muscle' for heart attacks?
Answer. Heart muscle dies the longer a blockage lasts.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
